title: Unit 02: Book-II Prose Part 2 (End of Term, Destroying Books, Hospital)
subject: english-12

questions.question: In 'End of Term', how does David Daiches describe his sensations on Monday mornings during school days?

options.A: Excitement to participate in school sports and debates
options.B: A heavy, dismal oppression at the thought of a whole week of school stretching ahead
options.C: Eagerness to meet his beloved headmaster

questions.explanation: Daiches describes waking up on Monday to the maid's voice as a dismal prison sentence, with five full days of arduous grind lying before him.

questions.question: What sound symbolized the arrival of the weekend and boundless happiness for young Daiches?

options.A: The school brass bell clanging at 3:30 PM on Friday and the ringing of his bicycle bell
options.B: The church choir singing Sunday hymns
options.C: The sound of rain pouring on the roof on Saturday
options.D: The postman knocking on Saturday morning

questions.explanation: Walking out of school on Friday afternoon was pure ecstasy; the weekend felt like a blessed oasis of freedom.

questions.question: Why did summer holidays in Daiches' childhood seem almost mythological and infinite in duration?

options.A: Because two months to a young schoolboy felt like a lifetime of sunny freedom
options.B: Because schools were closed for six months every year
options.C: Because he traveled to the Arctic Circle where the sun never set
options.D: Because he never had to return to school

questions.explanation: To a child, the two-month summer vacation seemed an eternity of sunny joy, though in reality it ended all too quickly.

questions.question: What childhood material desires remained unfulfilled for Daiches despite intense longing?

options.A: Owning a shiny tricycle and having pocket money to buy sweets freely
options.B: A horse and carriage to drive through Edinburgh
options.C: Gold watches and silk suits

questions.explanation: Daiches longed for a tricycle (and later a bicycle) and longed to spend pennies at sweet shops, but his family's modest budget kept pocket money scarce.

questions.question: In 'On Destroying Books', J.C. Squire argues that many people hoard bad or useless books because:

options.A: They believe paper will appreciate in commercial value.
options.B: They possess an irrational reverence for printed paper, feeling almost criminal if they throw a book away.
options.C: They intend to build massive private libraries.
options.D: Books are required by law to be preserved for censors.

questions.explanation: People treat printed books with quasi-religious respect, making them reluctant to destroy even worthless poetry or forgotten pamphlets.

questions.question: Why did the author find it impossible to burn his unwanted accumulation of books in his small London flat?

options.A: His landlord had banned gas stoves.
options.B: Books burn with immense difficulty, charring on the outside like stubborn granite while remaining white inside.
options.C: The smoke would activate municipal fire alarms.
options.D: The books were made of metal sheets.

questions.explanation: Closed books resist combustion; they smoulder, turn into charred crusts, and choke a domestic fireplace without actually burning.

questions.question: How did J.C. Squire decide to dispose of his heavy load of inferior books?

options.A: By donating them secretly to the British Museum
options.B: By packing them into a sack and dropping them into the River Thames at midnight
options.C: By burying them in Hyde Park
options.D: By tossing them onto the street from his second-floor balcony

questions.explanation: He stuffed the books into a large sack, hoisted it onto his shoulder after midnight, and walked toward Chelsea Bridge to drown them in the river.

questions.question: What terror seized the author while carrying his heavy sack along the Chelsea embankment at night?

options.A: Fear that a passing policeman would suspect him of carrying a murdered baby or stolen silverware
options.B: Fear that thieves would steal his precious poetry volumes
options.C: Fear that the sack would tear and books would fall into a sewer
options.D: Fear of ghosts from the London cemeteries

questions.explanation: A policeman loomed up in the fog, and Squire panicked that his nervous pacing and suspicious sack would look like the disposal of a corpse.

questions.question: What emotional reaction did Squire feel right after hearing the splash of his sack sinking into the Thames?

options.A: Vicious vindictive laughter
options.B: A sudden pang of pity and pathos for the unfortunate, forgotten authors lying in cold mud
options.C: Absolute indifference and boredom
options.D: Desire to jump in and rescue them

questions.explanation: He felt a tender sadness imagining the ambitious poets and writers lying abandoned at the cold bottom of the river.

questions.question: In 'The Man Who Was a Hospital', what induced Jerome K. Jerome to believe he was suffering from numerous ailments?

options.A: Visiting a pathology lab in Vienna
options.B: Reading a patent medicine circular describing symptoms of liver diseases
options.C: A medical examination by an army doctor
options.D: Attending university medical lectures as an auditor

questions.explanation: Jerome casually picked up a liver-pill circular and, upon reading the symptoms, foolishly convinced himself he had every condition described.

questions.question: When Jerome went to the British Museum reading room to study a specific ailment, what disease was he researching initially?

options.A: Hay fever
options.B: Typhoid
options.C: Cholera

questions.explanation: He looked up Hay Fever, but started browsing the medical book alphabetically from 'A' to 'Z', diagnosing himself with every single malady.

questions.question: What was the solitary disease in the medical dictionary that Jerome discovered he did NOT have?

options.A: Gout
options.B: Housemaid's Knee
options.C: Bright's disease

questions.explanation: He humorously felt slighted and indignant because, out of the entire medical encyclopedia, he did not suffer from 'Housemaid's Knee'.

questions.question: Why did Jerome consider himself an invaluable acquisition to the medical students of a teaching hospital?

options.A: He was wealthy enough to finance their medical laboratory.
options.B: Students would no longer need to walk around hospital wards; they could simply examine him to study all known diseases in a single patient.
options.C: He could teach them advanced surgical techniques.
options.D: He knew ancient herbal home remedies.

questions.explanation: He remarked that medical students could save months of ward rounds because examining him alone would give them diploma-level clinical experience.

questions.question: What practical prescription did Jerome's sensible doctor friend write for him?

options.A: Strong doses of arsenic, calomel, and opium
options.B: 1 lb beefsteak every 6 hours, a 10-mile walk every morning, bed at 11, and not to stuff his head with things he doesn't understand
options.C: Bed rest for two months in a darkened room
options.D: A trip to a Swiss tuberculosis sanatorium

questions.explanation: The doctor recognized hypochondria and prescribed simple food, physical exercise, regular sleep, and avoidance of medical literature.

questions.question: What witty reply did the chemist give Jerome when handed the doctor's prescription?

options.A: 'That will cost twenty guineas, sir.'
options.B: 'I am a chemist, sir, not a family hotel and a livery stable combined.'
options.C: 'This medicine is strictly out of stock.'

questions.explanation: Since the prescription contained beefsteak and lodging instructions rather than chemical compounds, the chemist politely declined.

questions.question: What tone predominates Jerome K. Jerome's essay 'The Man Who Was a Hospital'?

options.A: Melancholic and tragic
options.B: Light-hearted, self-deprecating satire and humor
options.C: Solemn and didactic scientific warning

questions.explanation: Jerome utilizes gentle irony, hyperbole, and comic absurdity to ridicule hypochondria and self-diagnosis.

questions.question: In 'End of Term', what does the phrase 'the maid's grim knock' signify?

options.A: The delivery of urgent telegrams
options.B: The daily rude awakening that terminated peaceful slumber and commenced the school day
options.C: A notification of school closure

questions.explanation: The maid knocking on the bedroom door was the dreaded signal that sleep was over and the harsh routine of school had begun.

questions.question: What was the psychological impact of Daiches receiving an unexpected half-holiday during school?

options.A: It was greeted with ecstatic delight because unearned, spontaneous freedom felt richer than scheduled vacations.
options.B: It caused anxiety because homework could not be handed in.
options.C: He spent it studying in the library.

questions.explanation: An unexpected half-holiday granted for a special occasion felt miraculously sweet and liberating to young students.

questions.question: What literary term describes the exaggeration: 'I crawled out a decrepit wreck... I had walked into that reading-room a healthy man, I crawled out an invalid'?

options.A: Metaphor
options.B: Hyperbole
options.C: Personification

questions.explanation: Exaggerating one's condition from healthy to near-death within an hour of reading is a textbook example of comic hyperbole.

questions.question: In 'On Destroying Books', Squire observes that throwing books away makes people feel like they are committing:

options.A: Sacrilege or murder
options.B: High treason against the Crown
options.C: A minor civil infraction

questions.explanation: People treat books as living spiritual entities, making discarding them feel akin to murder or sacrilege.

questions.question: What physical sensation did Squire experience while peering over the parapet of Chelsea Bridge?

options.A: A sudden urge to swim in the cold water
options.B: His heart pounded wildly and he hesitated repeatedly before mustering courage to fling the sack
options.C: He fell asleep on the bridge
options.D: He began reciting poetry aloud to passersby

questions.explanation: Paralyzed by guilt and fear of watchful eyes, he repeatedly stepped back before finally pushing the sack over the parapet.

questions.question: What is the primary moral takeaway of Jerome's encounter with the doctor?

options.A: Always seek five independent medical opinions.
options.B: Live a balanced, active, sensible life and never obsess over medical texts or imagined symptoms.
options.C: Never trust doctors who write in English rather than Latin.

questions.explanation: The doctor's prescription emphasizes practical outdoor exercise, plain food, adequate rest, and ignoring hypochondriac fears.

questions.question: In 'End of Term', Daiches mentions that in later life, when he had his own money, what changed about his childhood desires?

options.A: He bought hundred tricycles and sweets immediately.
options.B: The intense longing had evaporated, proving that desires must be fulfilled in their proper time to bring true joy.
options.C: He opened a candy store in Edinburgh.
options.D: He gave all his money to the school.

questions.explanation: When an adult finally has money to purchase childhood toys, the magical childhood craving is gone forever.

questions.question: Choose the correct meaning of the word 'hypochondriac':

options.A: A person suffering from chronic heart failure
options.B: A person who is abnormally anxious about their health and imagines illnesses they do not have
options.C: A physician specializing in bone surgery

questions.explanation: A hypochondriac suffers from irrational health anxiety and incessantly diagnoses nonexistent medical conditions in themselves.

questions.question: Identify the correct preposition: 'Jerome was seized _____ a sudden conviction that he had gout.'

options.A: at
options.B: with
options.C: by

questions.explanation: The established idiomatic phrase is 'seized with' when overtaken by an emotion, panic, or conviction.

questions.question: In 'On Destroying Books', Squire names several types of books that clutter homes, including:

options.A: Inferior poetry volumes, outdated reference manuals, and worthless ephemeral novels
options.B: Rare illuminated medieval manuscripts
options.C: Encyclopedias bound in gold leaf

questions.explanation: Squire refers to bad minor poetry, tenth-rate novels, and useless pamphlets that consume shelf space.

questions.question: What is the antonym of 'malady' as used in Jerome's essay?

options.A: Sickness
options.B: Affliction
options.C: Wellness / Robust health

questions.explanation: 'Malady' means a disease or ailment; its opposite is wellness, health, or robustness.

questions.question: In 'End of Term', how did the Daiches family spend their summer holidays?

options.A: By traveling to rural seaside villages in Scotland for walking and relaxation
options.B: By flying to Mediterranean resorts in Italy
options.C: By staying in Edinburgh attending summer school
options.D: By working in family manufacturing mills

questions.explanation: The family went to modest country houses or seaside spots in Scotland, spending leisurely days outdoors.

questions.question: What literary device is used in: 'The waters closed over them, and they slept in their muddy grave'?

options.A: Personification and metaphor
options.B: Litotes
options.C: Onomatopoeia

questions.explanation: Attributing sleep and a grave to drowned books personifies them and creates a poetic metaphor for their disposal.

questions.question: In 'The Man Who Was a Hospital', Jerome's pulse was beating at what ridiculous rate according to his self-examination?

options.A: It had stopped completely, or was racing at 147 beats a minute
options.B: Exactly 72 beats a minute
options.C: Around 50 beats a minute
options.D: His heart had shifted to his right ear

questions.explanation: He couldn't feel his pulse at first, then panicked and calculated it frantically at 147 beats per minute.

questions.question: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence according to formal grammar:

options.A: He said, "I am feeling unwell"; however, he refused to see a doctor.
options.B: He said, "I am feeling unwell;" however he refused to see a doctor.
options.C: He said "I am feeling unwell;" However, he refused to see a doctor.
options.D: He said, I am feeling unwell however, he refused to see a doctor.

questions.explanation: Proper punctuation places the semicolon outside the closing quotation mark when separating two independent clauses linked by 'however'.

questions.question: What is the synonym of 'inveterate' in the phrase 'an inveterate book collector'?

options.A: Occasional and reluctant
options.B: Habitual, chronic, and deeply ingrained
options.C: Amateurish and untrained

questions.explanation: 'Inveterate' describes a long-standing, habitual practice or behavior that is obstinately persistent.

questions.question: Which essayist wrote 'End of Term'?

options.A: David Daiches
options.B: Stephen Leacock
options.C: Sir Winston Churchill

questions.explanation: David Daiches, the renowned Scottish literary critic and historian, penned the autobiographical essay 'End of Term'.

questions.question: In 'On Destroying Books', what does the author conclude about the ultimate utility of weeding out bad books?

options.A: It makes room for new and better books, and saves one's heirs from being suffocated by junk.
options.B: It decreases paper consumption worldwide.
options.C: It lowers the tax bracket of the homeowner.
options.D: It allows bookcases to be sold at auctions.

questions.explanation: Destruction of rubbish is necessary to preserve living space and allow valuable literature to breathe on bookshelves.

questions.question: How did Jerome's doctor know his diagnosis without even taking his temperature?

options.A: He had seen Jerome's symptom list before in other hypochondriac patients who had read medical books.
options.B: He guessed by checking Jerome's horoscope.
options.C: He called the British Museum librarian.
options.D: He didn't know and merely took a wild guess.

questions.explanation: The doctor recognized the classic symptom of laypeople becoming terrified by medical dictionaries and prescribed wholesome living.
